questions.q: Which method draws a horizontal reference line, such as a sales target, across the whole axes?
options: ax.axvline()
ax.annotate()
ax.axhline()
ax.legend()
questions.explain: axhline draws a horizontal line at a chosen y value; axvline is its vertical counterpart.

options: Turns tick values such as 140 into labels like $140k
Rounds the underlying data to whole numbers
Adds a dollar-sign column to the DataFrame
Changes the y-axis range to 0-140
questions.explain: The format string controls how tick numbers are displayed; the data itself is unchanged.

questions.q: What is the purpose of ax.annotate(...) with arrowprops?
options: It changes the color of the line
It saves the figure to a file
It adds a legend
It points an arrow at a specific data point with explanatory text
questions.explain: annotate places text at xytext and draws an arrow to the data point xy, helping the reader notice the one moment that matters.

questions.q: What is the advantage of plt.rcParams and style sheets?
options: They make charts render faster
They let you set defaults once instead of styling every chart individually
They convert charts to interactive HTML
They add data to a chart
questions.explain: rcParams holds matplotlib's default settings and style sheets bundle them, so a project's charts stay consistent without repeated code.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should you decide whether to add a visual element to a chart?
options: Add it if it makes the chart look more impressive
Add every available option to the chart
Add it only if it helps the reader answer the question
Add it only if it is the default
questions.explain: Customize to clarify, not to decorate: targets, annotations and formatted axes help; gradients and heavy borders do not.
